item.title: Pro-Palestinian Activists Accused of Vandalizing Trump Resort Face Terrorism Accusation
item.description:
Scottish prosecutors will attempt to prove that pro-Palestinian activists accused of vandalizing one of President Trump’s Scottish golf resorts last year committed acts connected to terrorism. The move is the latest in a broadening effort in Britain to target protest groups with terrorism laws.

In March 2025, prosecutors say, seven members of the British protest group Palestine Action broke into the resort, Trump Turnberry. They dug up the turf and damaged the sprinklers. They sprayed the clubhouse with red paint. And they emblazoned “Gaza is not 4 sale” on part of the picturesque course.

All seven were charged with malicious damage to property and are set to face a judge in a preliminary hearing in Glasgow on Monday.

But the prosecutors’ 16-page indictment also argues that the vandalism was “aggravated by reason of having a terrorist connection,” which could lead to a harsher sentence if the accused were convicted.

In a social media post soon after the activists were arrested last year, Mr. Trump described them as “the terrorists who attacked the beautiful Turnberry” and said that “they did serious damage, and will hopefully be treated harshly.”

At the time, Palestine Action had claimed credit for carrying out several acts of vandalism, mostly against British sites connected to an Israeli weapons manufacturer, Elbit Systems. Three months after the Turnberry episode, the group said two of its members had vandalized planes at a British military base to protest what it described as Britain’s military support for Israel. The group posted footage of the episode online.

Days later, Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s government announced it would ban Palestine Action as a terrorist organization, a contentious move that prompted fierce debate over free speech and the right to protest.

The ban was the first time Britain had used antiterrorism powers against a group for “serious damage to property” rather than because of the use or threat of violence against people.

Legal experts said the indictment against the protesters draws on 25-year-old laws originally designed to severely stiffen sentences for people convicted of murder or other serious crimes in the course of a terror attack.

Prosecutors in Britain have begun aiming to apply the same provisions to political protesters, with varying degrees of success. In one case, four Palestine Action activists convicted of vandalizing a building owned by Elbit in Filton, England, were sentenced as terrorists. In another case, however, a judge rejected prosecutors’s efforts to apply a terrorism connection to Palestine Action protesters accused of breaking windows at a Barclays Bank branch.

Huda Ammori, the co-founder of Palestine Action, accused prosecutors of trying to advance the agendas of Mr. Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister of Israel, by pushing to sentence protesters as if they were terrorists.

“By hitting the profits of arms companies and by daring to spray paint on the golf course owned by the demagogue who has enabled Netanyahu’s crimes, we made powerful enemies,” she said in a statement. “The British government chose to appease them by criminalizing us as ‘terrorists.’”

That designation led to the arrests of several thousand protesters for holding signs that said: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.” The terrorism law used against Palestine Action criminalizes the wearing, display or publication of anything that expresses support for a banned group.

On Wednesday, the Trump administration also designated Palestine Action as a terrorist organization as part of what it called “Action Against Violent Far-Left Terrorist Networks,” saying in a statement that the decision “complements the U.K.’s proscription.”

Jonathan Hall, an independent adviser to the British government on terrorism laws, said the authorities were right to want more tools to prevent terrorism, which is broadly defined in British law and can include serious damage to property. But he said the government was grappling with when to apply those legal tools.

“The really tricky thing,” he said, “and I’ve got no brilliant answer for this, is where do you draw the line?”

Amnesty International has accused the British government of overreach. In the case of the vandalism at Turnberry, Felix Jakens, director of communications at the human rights organization, said that it was “completely disproportionate to equate painting on a golf course with terrorism.”

“A terrorism sentence stays with you for life,” he added, “and it’s shocking that the defendants could face such severe punishments for this nonviolent protest.”

While in office, Mr. Starmer rejected charges that his government was endangering free speech by targeting protesters.

In May, he said that he wanted “tougher action” taken toward protesters who chant certain slogans like “globalize the intifada” that cause fear among British Jews. The Metropolitan Police in London previously announced that they would arrest protesters for using the phrase.

Andy Burnham, who replaced Mr. Starmer as prime minister, has not directly confronted the issue since taking office last month. Some members of his Labour Party have made clear that they believe he should take a stand against the overuse of terrorism laws.

In February, judges at England’s High Court ruled that the government’s ban of Palestine Action had been unlawful, saying it was disproportionate and breached the right to protest. But he Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in June. The Supreme Court will consider the case in November.

item.title: Fears of a Second Flood Grow as Rescue Efforts Continue in Nepal
item.description:
As emergency workers searched Himalayan valleys on Thursday for survivors of a colossal flood that killed hundreds of people, the Nepali and Chinese authorities warned that a second flood might be coming — with rescuers most at risk, according to an expert.

The landslide that set off Wednesday’s flood clogged the river system and created a barrier lake close to the border between Nepal and the Tibet region of China, the Chinese Ministry of Water Resources said Thursday evening. It said that rain forecast to fall over the next three days could more than double the lake’s water volume to over 176 million cubic feet, the equivalent of about 2,000 Olympic-size swimming pools.

The risk that the new lake could breach its rocky barrier and wreak havoc downstream was “high,” the ministry said, potentially causing areas such as the Gyirong border crossing, which had already been decimated by floodwaters, to be “struck by disaster again.”

The lake had already started to overflow on Thursday, forcing rescue efforts in Tibet to stop and sending water at speeds of more than 120 miles per hour into the same river that flooded a day earlier, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Friday morning.

Nepal’s disaster management agency on Thursday urged people to move away from riverbanks because of the risk of a second flood.

Another deluge would track the same path as the first, posing the most risk to people on search-and-rescue missions, said Austin Lord, an anthropologist and senior fellow at the Stimson Center in Washington, who has studied natural disasters in Nepal.

A second flood would be another challenge for rescue and assistance efforts already forced to navigate destroyed infrastructure and damaged communication lines. “Warnings of potential renewed floods are complicating an already challenging operation,” said David Fisher, head of delegation for International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies in Nepal.

While the flood would most likely be smaller and significantly less deadly, Mr. Lord said, the volume of water in the new lake is “not insignificant.” He compared its potential impact to that of a flood that hit the same area last year, killing at least eight people, destroying a key border bridge and disrupting trade between Nepal and China.

“We have no way of knowing how the dynamics would play out,” Mr. Lord said. “The area is so freshly volatile.”

But governments, residents and rescuers would have a crucial advantage this time: a heads-up.

“They’re running models of potential floods and visually monitoring the growth,” said Alton C. Byers, a senior research associate at the Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research at the University of Colorado, Boulder. “They can warn people.”

The Himalayas are dotted with thousands of glacial lakes, posing a constant flood risk if large, falling debris crashes into them. The region is known for being prone to natural disasters.

Scientists have said the deadly flood on Wednesday was probably caused by a massive rock landslide colliding with a glacier falling from the high mountains.

Mr. Lord said scientists were also monitoring what seems to be yet another new body of water forming at the initial impact point below the north face of Langtang Lirung, a mountain in Nepal near the border with China.

“It seems to have created a glacial lake that’s growing in size,” Mr. Lord said. “It may overtop or breach at some point in the coming days.”

Lily Kuo and Mujib Mashal contributed reporting.

item.title: Yielding on French Could Restart Trade Talks, Canadian Officials Say
item.description:
Canada’s minister responsible for trade with the United States said on Thursday that a pledge from a Trump administration official to not challenge Canadian laws around French language and Canadian culture could provide an opening to renew negotiations.

Trade talks between the United States and Canada, its second-largest trading partner, collapsed late last week into a battle that Prime Minister Mark Carney compared to war, as the Trump administration announced severe tariffs and Canada retaliated with its own.

After Mr. Carney revealed that the United States’ designs on French language measures had contributed to the breakdown of negotiations, the issue has dominated reports about the trade dispute from French language news outlets based in Quebec, and further fueled animosity across the country toward President Trump.

Mr. Trump may have eroded any trade talk good will established on Thursday, when, speaking from the Oval Office, he signed an executive order to rename Lake Ontario, one of the Great Lakes shared by both countries, to “Lake America.”

Among the points that the trade negotiators clashed over were Canadian laws and regulations protecting the use of French in daily life and promoting French-language movies and shows, as well as general Canadian culture online. The minister, Dominic LeBlanc, alluded to those rules on Thursday, referring to Canadian laws that require online streaming services to make it easier for users to “discover” shows and movies in French.

“Canada welcomes that the U.S. is now withdrawing its positions on discoverability and labeling and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future U.S. trade actions,” Mr. LeBlanc said in a social media post. “We look forward to further constructive U.S. clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty.”

Mr. LeBlanc appeared to be reacting to comments made by Jamieson Greer, the United States Trade Representative, in an interview with CBC News, the Canadian public broadcaster, that aired on Wednesday.

In the interview, Mr. Greer said that laws and regulations to make it easier to find French content on streaming services had been “highlighted” by the American side, but he said that they were not a make-or-break issue.

But on Thursday afternoon, Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, was less diplomatic about the role of language during the failed trade talks. Speaking to reporters in Washington, he said, “Do I care about how the Québécois speak? I mean, what could matter less to America? We don’t care. So the fact is: we never brought those words up.”

Reporting by The New York Times found that hard line interventions in the trade talks by Mr. Lutnick on the key issues of steel, aluminum and auto ultimately brought on their failure.

In the interview, Mr. Greer said, “President Trump, myself and the U.S. government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada.” He added: “There is no way we would let a good deal go by for something like this. This is not something where we push hard or condition or red line.”

Mr. Greer’s statement was a shift from the sometimes acrimonious exchange of words across the border in recent days.

The equal status of French and English is mandated in Canada’s Constitution, making it virtually impossible for Canada to bargain over them, although the potential political backlash to such changes in Quebec is an equally powerful restraint. On Thursday, Christine Fréchette, the premier of Quebec, opened campaigning for a provincial election to be held in October by saying that Mr. Trump is her “principal adversary” in the campaign.

“We are being attacked head-on, like never before, by our largest economic partner,” she said. “We’ll have to defend ourselves, you have to know how to defend yourself.”

On the matter of tariffs, Canada made changes of its own on Thursday. When the country imposed retaliatory levies on hundreds of American goods earlier this week, following Mr. Trump’s 50 percent tariffs on hundreds on Canadian products, one category stood out. Canada’s list, which covers about $20 billion in imports from the U.S., contained dozens of kinds of fish, fresh and frozen, including herring, shell fish, tuna and flat fish, all identified by their scientific names in Latin.

Mr. Trump had not targeted Canada’s seafood sector with tariffs, puzzling some in the fisheries industry who viewed the move by Mr. Carney as a provocation. Canada’s tariffs come into effect on Sept. 8.

“He’s starting something that Donald Trump didn’t start,” said Chris Poirier, a seafood buyer in the fishing village of Chéticamp, Nova Scotia, adding that he thought it was counterproductive for Mr. Carney to “go after the fishing industry.”

On Thursday, however, the government of Canada said in a social media post that it had changed its mind and American fish would continue to enter Canada tariff free.

The fishing industries of Atlantic Canada and New England are as integrated as the auto industries in Ontario and the United States, said Stewart Lamont, a lobster industry expert in Nova Scotia.

By including Canadian seafood products — particularly lobster, the sector’s most valuable export — in its tariffs package, Canada looked to inflict pain on a state like Maine, he said. However, the move risked driving down the price of lobster and triggering job losses.

In a statement, John Fragos, the spokesman for François-Philippe Champagne, Canada’s finance minister, said the list was revamped and fish were purged “in the interest of strengthening Canada’s sectors and our tariff response — and to better match the American tariffs.”

item.title: Prince William Is Still Silent About His Brother, Harry. Can That Last?
item.description:
Prince William, the future king of England, has said nothing publicly about his brother’s decision to return home. Not on social media. Not through a royal spokesman. Not a word.

Since last week, the British news media has exploded into a speculative frenzy about where Prince Harry and his family will live, what he will do, and most of all, whether he will reconcile with his estranged brother. William’s silence hangs heavy over the monarchy he will eventually inherit.

The heir to the throne has worked for years to show that he will be a new kind of monarch, more in tune with the modern world than his father or grandmother could be. In public campaigns, he has encouraged men, especially, to confront mental health challenges, to abandon the “stiff upper lip” that is so typically British, and to be open to the idea of seeking therapy.

Earlier this year, he let it be known that he maintains a “quiet faith” and wants to form “a strong and meaningful bond” with the Church of England when he is king.

“Forgiveness is at the heart of Christian morality,” said Ed Owens, a royal historian. “There would be great magnanimity on his part if he would look like the bigger person.”

And yet, the royal rift between Harry and the sibling he used to call Willy remains wide, by all accounts. There is little evidence that anything has been resolved since the pair’s intense clashes in the months before Harry and his wife, Meghan, left Britain, some of which Harry wrote about in his memoir, “Spare.”

“He grabbed me by the collar, ripping my necklace, and he knocked me to the floor,” Harry wrote about one physical altercation with William in 2019, which Harry claimed took place in the cottage he shared with Meghan. “I landed on the dogs’ bowl, which cracked under my back, the pieces cutting into me. I lay there for a moment, dazed, then got to my feet and told him to get out.”

Kensington Palace has long refused to comment on that accusation, though royal watchers have said that William denies that a physical altercation ever took place. It is clear from what hasn’t happened — any public conversation between the two men since Queen Elizabeth’s funeral four years ago — that the breach remains deep.

In 1997, the brothers endured the tragedy of their mother Diana’s death at the age of 36 when her car crashed while paparazzi were chasing it in Paris. William was 15 and Harry 12. In “Spare,” Harry wrote of the “decade of unrelenting pain” he experienced as he tried to make sense of the loss.

“Both William and Harry have to be carrying the trauma from their childhood and that will complicate their reactions to anything,” said Catherine Mayer, the author of “Divide and Rule: Royal Women and Their Battles.” “It made them unbelievably close, but it also means that the feelings they have for each other are bound to be strong in all sorts of ways.”

Stronger, even, than the anger that clearly existed between Harry and his father, King Charles III, after the prince arrived in the United States and aired the royal family’s dirty laundry in interviews, documentaries and a tell-all book, accusing some in the family of racism and bullying aimed at Meghan.

At the time, Buckingham Palace said in a statement that “some recollections may vary” but that the accusations were being “taken very seriously and will be addressed by the family privately.” The statement also said that Harry and Meghan “will always be much loved family members.”

In 2025, Harry met with his father for tea at the king’s London residence, in what appeared to be the first step toward healing their rift. Last month, Charles and Queen Camilla met privately with Harry, Meghan and their two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5, at Highgrove House in Gloucestershire. By all accounts — none of them detailed or specific — the meeting went well.

Last week, a person familiar with the king’s response to the family’s move back to Britain said that Charles “welcomes the opportunity to see more of the Sussex family in a private and personal capacity.”

No such sentiment was released by anyone close to William. When asked for comment, Kensington Palace, which represents William and Catherine, said it did not comment on anything related to Harry and Meghan.

Since Queen Elizabeth’s funeral, Harry has only been in the same place as William twice, once for his father’s coronation as king in May 2023, and again when both men attended a memorial service for their uncle, Lord Robert Fellowes, in August of 2024. On both occasions, Harry and William did not appear to interact with each other at all.

Last week, people close to Harry and Meghan made it known that the couple were moving back and had enrolled their children in school in Britain.

The explanation offered by The Sun and The Daily Telegraph, the two British newspapers that each claimed to have the story exclusively, was simple enough. The exiled prince and his wife wanted to bring their children up in the peace and quiet of the British countryside where Harry has some of his fondest memories.

“HARRY & MEG COMING HOME,” the Sun headline blared on Wednesday. “Royals move back from US to raise kids in UK.”

The family reportedly arrived in Britain on a private plane on Wednesday, though their spokesman declined to confirm it. At the time of writing, there was no public welcome home or statement of well wishes from Charles or William.

The question is how long that silence can last, especially from the country’s future king.

Now that Harry is back, William will be peppered with questions about whether, and when, they might reconnect. Will Harry and Meghan and the children be invited to the royal family’s Christmas celebrations? Will Harry join William — even as a non-working royal — at any public events? What about their children, who have spent almost no time together?

The answers may depend on how the next few weeks and months unfold. Some royal watchers have predicted that Harry and Meghan will try to keep a low profile at first to minimize confrontations.

“What we’re probably going to see is a couple laying relatively low, steadily trying to rebuild their public images,” Mr. Owens said. “And doing so discreetly. They’re not coming here for another fight or for more acrimony.”

And yet, Harry’s presence nearby may end up irritating William, who has had no in-town competition for attention since his brother moved away. Harry is expected to make some public appearances in the coming weeks, including in his role as the founder of the Invictus Games, a sporting event for wounded military personnel and veterans.

Ms. Mayer, the author, said that William would benefit in the long run from a reconciliation with his brother because Harry and Meghan remain popular with a younger generation that is already wary of the stodgy, old-fashioned royalty that has existed under Charles and Elizabeth.

“If William and Harry were different sorts of people, and they’re not, you might think it perfectly plausible that they would find a way to mend fences for the sake of the monarchy,” she said.

“But this is not that ideal world,” Ms. Mayer added, “and so who knows?”

item.title: Qatari Prime Minister Travels to Tehran as Iran War Nears Six-Month Mark
item.description:
The prime minister of Qatar, a key mediator in the U.S. war with Iran, was in Tehran on Thursday for talks with senior Iranian officials as the conflict nears the six-month mark with no clear end in sight.

The prime minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, met with the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi.

Discussions were focused on fostering the “conditions conducive to dialogue” and “upholding freedom of navigation” in the Strait of Hormuz, the Qatari Foreign Ministry said in a statement.

Sheikh Mohammed also met with Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and the country’s lead negotiator in talks with Washington, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, according to Iranian state media.

The visit comes at a moment of heightened tension between Iran and Qatar. An Iranian general recently accused the Qataris of detaining three pilots who were shot down early in the war, a claim that Qatar denies.

After the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, Qatar has faced more than 700 missile and drone attacks that it blamed on Tehran, including strikes on natural gas facilities. Last month, Qatar accused Iran of targeting one of its gas tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Qatar, which hosts a major U.S. military base, helped broker a cease-fire between the United States and Iran in June that was intended to pause hostilities and lead to negotiations toward a lasting peace.

That agreement has since unraveled, largely because of disputes over the strait, a crucial waterway for oil and gas that runs along Iran’s southern coast and that both Tehran and Washington have blockaded.

For weeks, Iran and Oman, which also abuts the Strait of Hormuz, have been in talks about introducing a temporary route through the waterway, but no agreement has yet been announced.

The Qatari Foreign Ministry’s statement said that the proposed route in the strait, along with demining efforts in the waterway, were discussed during talks in Tehran on Thursday.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, said that Sheikh Mohammed’s visit would focus on Qatar’s continuing mediation efforts. The general who claimed the Qataris had detained the pilots, Seyed Mohammad Bagherzadeh, said this month that the men were flying Su-24 fighter jets in an operation on March 2, days after the outbreak of the war. He said that their planes had been hit by “enemy defenses” and that the pilots had ejected and had later been captured by the Qatari authorities.

Qatari officials have expressed surprise at the Iranian claim. Majed al-Ansari, a Foreign Ministry spokesman, said in a news conference last week that Tehran had been invited to send a technical team to Doha, the Qatari capital, to review search operations for the pilots but had not done so.

The Iranian Foreign Ministry said on Monday that the fate of the pilots remained unclear. Mr. Pezeshkian’s office said on Thursday that the issue of the missing pilots was raised in the president’s meeting with Sheikh Mohammed, but did not elaborate.

Despite the recent tensions, Qatar, alongside Pakistan, has continued to try to mediate in the conflict between the United States and Iran.

Officials from Pakistan were in Tehran on Monday, with one member of the delegation describing “very positive and productive” meetings toward restoring the terms of the cease-fire agreement brokered in June. Oman’s foreign minister was also in Iran this week to discuss shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

The flurry of diplomacy this week comes after the Trump administration announced a raft of new economic restrictions against 60 Iranian and Iran-linked entities, calling the measures an “economic D-Day.”

item.title: After Whiskey With His Captors, Cuban Dissident Lands in a Miami Maelstrom
item.description:
It has been a busy summer for the Cuban artist and former political prisoner Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara.

Upon finishing a five-year prison sentence in Cuba, he was moved to a beach-front government safe house, where he said he drank beer and Chinese whiskey with state security agents. Then came a surprisingly hard part: exile in Miami, where within days his hero’s welcome turned into a social media maelstrom.

The reproaches came soon after he arrived last month, particularly from online influencers.

He looked too healthy to have spent five years in prison, critics said. Since when does the Cuban government let prisoners paint in their cells — or take thousands of paintings into exile, they wondered. And he stunned audiences when, in an interview with an 87-year-old former political prisoner, he talked crudely about sex.

“I’m really not trying to be provocative,” Mr. Otero Alcántara, 38, said later in a voice mail message. “I am provocative.”

Overnight, Mr. Otero Alcántara became a living testament to the tangled realities of the Cuban diaspora: generations of exiles and their families, many of whom have never set foot on the island, as well as recent arrivals who grew up under communist rule. Unlike many diaspora members who are wealthy and white, Mr. Otero is Black and has working-class roots, the son of a welder and an office worker from El Cerro, a gritty Havana neighborhood.

So on one side, Mr. Otero Alcántara had a rapturous reception, from figures as varied as Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a member of the hip-hop group Orishas and hundreds who came to see his work unveiled at Miami’s Freedom Tower.

But he also faced a flurry of negative reactions, so fast and so harsh that some experts wondered whether Cuban state security was surreptitiously running a propaganda campaign to tarnish a rising star of the dissident movement.

Experts said that the artist probably was afforded special treatment as a prisoner because officials knew that he would, like other dissidents, receive significant attention after he was released. Letting him leave the country looking healthy and with paintings could help discredit other political prisoners who reported abuses, and perhaps improve Cuba’s image around the world, they said.

Last week, Mr. Otero Alcántara acknowledged that some people had gone as far as suggesting he worked for Cuba’s intelligence directorate, known as the G2.

“In Cuba, the dictatorship accuses me of being a C.I.A. agent. In Miami, some accuse me of being a G2 agent,” he posted on social media. “Someone has serious identity issues.”

The Cuban government did not respond to requests for comment about his release, but in the past it has accused him and his movement of being “trained and supported” by the U.S. Embassy in Havana.

His profile as an irreverent artist and dissident grew after 2018, when Cuba banned cultural activity not authorized by the state. That ignited the most organized uprising from the arts community in Cuba’s history, said Coco Fusco, a friend of the artist and professor at the Cooper Union, an art school in New York.

Mr. Otero Alcántara used performance art to connect directly with working-class frustrations.

On one occasion, he wore a hard hat and stood under dilapidated balconies, highlighting the risk to children after three were killed from falling masonry. Another time, he stood outside a new, $500-a-night luxury hotel, selling raffle tickets for a night’s stay.

His political activism expanded through the San Isidro Movement, a loose collective of artists and activists that emerged as one of Cuba’s most visible dissident groups.

Cuban state security agents accused him of doing the work of the island’s “imperialist” enemies. His appeal to many downtrodden Afro-Cubans posed an unusual threat to the government, Ms. Fusco said.

“They fear his kind of charismatic power over that sector of the population,” she said.

Dozens of detentions and interrogations followed, as well as constant surveillance outside his house.

In 2021, following major anti-government protests in which more than 1,500 people were arrested, he was charged with public disorder, accused of defaming the Cuban flag.

He served the five years. After his release last month, while his supporters in Miami publicly declared him missing, he spent time at the safe house awaiting a U.S. visa.

In an interview Mr. Otero Alcántara gave to TV Martí, a journalist posited that he was in all likelihood surveilled there, and asked what those videos might show.

Mr. Otero Alcántara acknowledged in the interview that he had been accompanied by his son and girlfriend, and that he had drunk with state agents.

It went downhill from there.

He then did a live social media interview with Ángel de Fana, the elderly former political prisoner, who told him that in his day, no self-respecting political prisoner would have accepted treats. The conversation devolved when Mr. Otero Alcántara made vulgar references to women and sex.

In an interview with The New York Times, Mr. de Fana called Mr. Otero Alcántara “brave.” But he added that some of the criticisms against him, particularly of how crudely he spoke about sex, were self-inflicted.

“We weren’t in a private conversation; he was transmitting live,” Mr. de Fana said. “It’s not correct. He doesn’t respect the women he was with.”

Mr. Otero Alcántara said that many exiles had anticipated he would emerge malnourished and telling horror stories.

“People expect something else, expect me to say that the dictatorship took me, broke my bones and gouged my eyes out,” he said. “Here I am with my eyes and my bones fine. It doesn’t mean that what happened to me wasn’t dramatically traumatic. The problem is that people understand violence only as when you get hit with a stick, when you get hurt — when that’s just a symbol.”

Mr. Otero Alcántara does not fit neatly into what many Cuban exiles have long expected of a high-profile activist, experts said. He came up as an untrained artist, rather than a political activist as such.

The “friendly fire” he has experienced underscores an intransigence among many Cubans both on the island and in South Florida, said Ted Henken, a Baruch College scholar who wrote letters to the U.S. government in support of the artist’s humanitarian parole application.

“There’s almost like a script you are expected to follow,” he said, “genuflecting at the temple of exile and engaging in a kind of performance of martyrdom.”

Mr. Otero Alcántara said many people received him warmly, which was a welcome respite from prison. He added that he would keep speaking his mind, even if others didn’t want to hear.

He plans to spend the next two months as a resident artist at El Espacio 23, a studio in Miami’s Wynwood arts district. He may also take his works, which provide a rare glimpse of life inside a Cuban prison, on tour as testimony of Cubans’ suffering and resistance.

Exposed to humid prison conditions, some pieces will need touching up and others may be beyond salvation, he said. Many were composed on scraps of paper, like the insides of unfolded cigarette packs or sketchbooks sent by family and friends.

He recently invited a small group to observe the unpacking of his “prison archive,” the works carefully wrapped in acid-free conservation paper.

He held up dozens of paintings, showing images like a distorted prison cell, prisoners in an illusory swimming pool, and labyrinthine walls. He explained how he felt it was his duty as an artist to keep painting while incarcerated, both as an act of protest and to provide a glimpse into the suffering, isolation and boredom of his fellow prisoners.

“These are all prints of my state of mind,” he said.

The dark and visceral depictions of prison life, ranging from the erotic to the scatological, also unnerved the guards and helped stop their harassment of him, he said.

He unrolled a large pastel work on creased brown paper showing a naked man pouring water over his head while clouds of mosquitoes swarmed.

He seemed to leave prison with remarkably little bitterness.

“Refusing to give in to hate is crucial,” he said, “because that’s exactly what the regime — the dictatorship — wants: for anxiety to take you over, for hate to consume you and for you to turn into a toxic person.”

item.title: Canada Hires 48 Scholars Away From Top U.S. Universities
item.description:
Twenty-one universities in Canada announced on Thursday the hiring of dozens of researchers to join their top academic ranks, poaching the majority of the recruits from the United States.

Of the incoming 64 researchers, 48 will leave American campuses including Harvard, Yale and M.I.T., and the remainder are from Europe, Asia and Australia.

Turmoil in American academia, precipitated by a crackdown on prestigious universities by the Trump administration and attacks on scientific research groups, has allowed Canada a rare opportunity to lure some of those schools’ top minds north.

Their hiring is paid for through a Canadian government investment of more than 500 million Canadian dollars (about $364 million) in research fields that are strategically important, from global warming to artificial intelligence. The program was announced last December as part of a broader $1.2 billion investment in Canadian innovation projects, with a second round of 63 academics to be hired next year.

While scientists often shy away from political discourse, some are saying the Trump administration’s assault on science is behind their departure.

“I used to live in the country that I thought was the most enthusiastic about the prospects for science improving the human condition, of any country in the world,” said Phillip Zamore, the chair of RNA Therapeutics Institute at the University of Massachusetts. “And I woke up one day and that wasn’t true anymore.”

He has been recruited to McGill University in Montreal, which has also hired five other researchers, and will join the medical faculty.

“If scientists don’t stand up for truth, no one will,” Dr. Zamore said.

The Canada-bound brain drain from U.S. institutions began last year as the Trump administration put forward policies that targeted foreign students, academic freedom and funding for equity-related programs.

Kevin Hall, a nutrition scientist who left the U.S. National Institutes of Health last year, accusing federal officials of censoring his research on ultraprocessed foods, has been hired at the University of Ottawa.

“While certain countries are cutting research and turning their back on academic freedom, we’re doubling down on science,” Mélanie Joly, Canada’s industry minister, told reporters at the announcement, in Vancouver, of the new university hiring. She billed it as the world’s “largest talent attraction” project. The European Union has made a similar push.

“Years from now, we will look back at today’s announcement, and we will be able to seize the lasting impact of our choices,” Ms. Joly said.

Unpredictable decisions about funding prompted Seth Guikema, a professor in civil and environmental engineering, who has specialized in natural hazards modeling at the University of Michigan, to look elsewhere. His work focuses on how climate hazards inequitably affect communities, and that work has become harder to fund, he said.

“Every country sets its priorities in terms of what is going to get funded, and I think Canada has done a very good job of supporting research in areas that really matter to society,” said Dr. Guikema, who will start at Western University in London, Ontario in January.

The University of Toronto has also recruited six academics, including Sara Seager, a Canadian astrophysicist from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Universities in Canada are the latest pathway for some Americans to leave the United States, citing the Trump administration’s policies. Canada has also expanded citizenship eligibility for people who can prove their Canadian ancestry, resulting in thousands of applications from Americans.

item.title: Greenlandic Women Will Finally Get Money for Forced Contraception
item.description:
This has been a long time coming.

Starting in the 1960s and for decades after, the Danish government implanted intrauterine devices in Greenlandic women and girls. Some of them were as young as 12, and many had no idea what was being done to them.

For years afterward, they carried around their discomfort, health problems and shame, often in silence.

On Thursday, Danish lawmakers finally took a major step toward compensating the women, passing a bill that offers those who qualify a one-time payment of 300,000 Danish kroner, or about $47,000.

“It is something positive against a very sad background,” said Naaja Nathanielsen, one of two Greenlanders in Denmark’s Parliament.

The move comes at a time when Denmark is bending over backward to keep Greenland onside. The gigantic Arctic island, three times the size of Texas, is a semiautonomous Danish territory and a fixation of President Trump, who has threatened to annex it.

Denmark has deployed just about all the tools it has, even preparing to blow up airfields in Greenland, to keep Mr. Trump away. Part of the Danish strategy is to solidify its bonds with Greenlanders. Although many Greenlanders have said they want to stick with Denmark, the relationship is still riddled with lingering questions, especially regarding the contraception campaign.

Widely known as the “Spiral Case,” after the shape of the intrauterine devices that were used, the campaign has remained an upsetting symbol of what Greenlanders consider generations of mistreatment by Danes. As part of the Danish government’s decades-long effort to slow down Greenland’s population growth, Danish doctors invited Greenlandic women and girls for checkups. Then, often secretly, they implanted the intrauterine devices, or IUDs, for birth control.

In many cases, the women and girls found out what was inside them only years later, after they started having health complications. Some were left infertile for life.

The campaign continued into the 1990s, and experts say they believe that Greenland’s population of around 57,000 would be much bigger if it had never happened. After decades of silence, some women stepped forward a few years ago to speak out. That led to a cascade of accounts that revealed just how damaging and widespread the practice had been — more than 4,000 Greenlandic women were affected, according to an authoritative report published last year.

Mette Frederiksen, Denmark’s prime minister, offered an official apology, saying, “On behalf of Denmark, I would like to say sorry.” Another government-commissioned report on the legal aspects and whether the campaign should be considered a genocide is expected to come out this week.

Women seeking compensation will have to submit an application describing what they had experienced in detail, the Danish authorities said. “We know that it can be sensitive for the woman to describe what happened, but we need to hear what the woman can remember in order to make a decision in the case,” said Trine Berner Madsen, an official involved in the process.

Medical records are not required, although applicants can supply them to bolster their case.

Aana Uulat Bach, a retired teacher living in Nuuk, Greenland’s capital, said the compensation measure brought her “a huge relief.”

“The scars inside us will still be there,” she said in a telephone interview on Thursday. “But now we have the opportunity to move forward.”

Ms. Bach, 64, said she was fitted with an IUD when she was around 13 and later suffered fertility problems, including blocked fallopian tubes, as well as two pregnancies outside her uterus, which can be life-threatening.

Despite that, she has one son, whom she described as a “miracle.”

“My fight over this case is coming to an end,” she said “We no longer have to keep wondering whether we will ever be recognized.”
